1	# Headless browser
2	
3	## Getting a browser
4	
5	- **Resolve the binary out of the environment; never let the driver download one.** A container
6	  or runner image that already ships a browser is the normal case, and the driver's own registry
7	  download is slow, often blocked, and pins a build you did not choose. Look for an explicit
8	  override variable first, then the image's browser root, then fall through to the driver's own
9	  resolution — and prefer the driver's `-core` package, which bundles no browser at all. The
10	  image's build number need not match the driver's own pin for the browser to launch. Never
11	  hardcode the version-stamped path you found by looking: it moves with the next image, and the
12	  failure lands on whoever rebuilds rather than on whoever wrote it.
13	
14	- **A fresh install of the driver package is the same danger from upstream.** Reinstalling the
15	  package to fix an import error just as easily resolves to a newer release than the one paired
16	  with the environment's pinned browser — it then hunts for a browser build the image was never
17	  given and fails asking for a network install the sandbox cannot make. A reinstall run from the
18	  repo root instead of a scratchpad can dodge that failure outright (a version happens to
19	  resolve that works) and still cost you: it dirties the tracked `package.json`, its lockfile and
20	  `node_modules`, which then need a manual revert before anything can be committed. Resolve the
21	  already-installed package by its global path instead of adding a second copy, at any depth in
22	  the tree.
23	
24	- **When a page depends on a third-party library loaded from a CDN you have not vendored,
25	  stub the library's own API surface rather than trying to make the CDN reachable.** A default
26	  network abort (above) leaves the page's global for that library undefined, so every call into
27	  it throws and the render comes back empty — indistinguishable from a product bug unless you
28	  know the cause. Grep the code under test for the handful of calls it actually makes (a mapping
29	  or charting library often boils down to a handful of constructors and methods) and install a
30	  minimal no-op implementation of just those as an init script, before the page's own scripts run.
31	
32	- **A committed pixel golden is only comparable under the exact build that rendered it.** Two
33	  browsers a version apart rasterise text and shadows differently, so a comparison across them
34	  measures the renderer, not the product. Where the output is compared pixel by pixel, read the
35	  installed driver version at launch and **refuse to run** on any other, naming the pinned one in
36	  the error; where it is not — a build artifact, a behavioural assertion — let the build float
37	  and spend nothing on pinning it.
38	
39	- **Pinning is what buys a zero-diff browser golden — budget for the whole recipe or accept a
40	  tolerance.** A browser screenshot is not bit-stable across machines by default, which is why
41	  the general advice is a small tolerance. It *can* be made bit-stable, and the price is this
42	  pack's next two sections in full: the pinned build, a font jail, and the rasterisation flags.
43	  Take all of it or take the tolerance; a half-applied recipe gives a zero-diff gate that fails
44	  on someone else's machine for reasons no one can read off the diff.
45	
46	## The page's world is an input — replace all of it
47	
48	- **Serve the page from a fake origin you fulfil from disk, and abort anything you did not
49	  name.** Intercepting at the browser needs no server process, no port and no free-port race,
50	  and it reaches *every* request the page makes rather than the ones an application-level mock
51	  happens to know about. Make the default arm an abort: a new external dependency then breaks
52	  the run loudly instead of quietly adding real network to a run meant to be hermetic.
53	
54	- **Use an `https` fake origin.** Geolocation and several other capabilities exist only on a
55	  secure origin, and a page served over `http` silently takes the denied path instead. Routes
56	  are fulfilled before any connection is attempted, so no certificate is involved and nothing
57	  has to be trusted.
58	
59	- **Route a vendored third-party asset host-agnostically.** A stylesheet you serve in place of a
60	  CDN copy still resolves *its own* relative URLs against the host it was served from, so the
61	  font or image files it references arrive addressed to that CDN. Match those follow-up requests
62	  on the path alone, on any host, or the sheet loads and every asset it names 404s — which
63	  renders as a silent fallback rather than an error.
64	
65	- **Know which knobs are fixed at context creation and which are per page.** Locale, timezone,
66	  viewport, device scale factor, geolocation and permissions belong to the browser *context* and
67	  cannot be changed once it exists — so proving that a product reads a fixed zone rather than
68	  the device's takes **two** contexts, not one page reconfigured twice. The clock, seeded
69	  randomness and injected scripts are per page.
70	
71	- **A command-line window-size flag is not a viewport — a narrow one does not test the narrow
72	  layout.** Ask a browser's *CLI* for a phone-sized window and it renders the page at a clamped
73	  width and crops the overflow, without applying the media queries the width should have
74	  triggered. The output looks exactly like a horizontal-overflow bug in every section of a page
75	  that has none, and the instinct is to go hunting through the CSS for the offender. Only a
76	  context or page created with an explicit viewport puts the page in that layout. Reserve the
77	  CLI screenshot for the width the window happens to be, and give it a virtual-time budget that
78	  outlasts the page's entrance animations, or sections capture mid-transition and read as broken
79	  when they are fine.
80	
81	- **Install every fake as an init script, so it runs before the page's first script.** A stub
82	  installed after load has already lost every call made during boot. Seeded randomness, storage
83	  seeds, and any API you are replacing all belong there.
84	
85	- **Freezing CSS animation does not freeze the Web Animations API.** Zeroing
86	  `animation-duration` and `transition-duration` stops declarative animation and nothing else;
87	  anything driven through `element.animate` keeps running, and a capture races it. Stub the
88	  method so every such animation resolves on its end state immediately.
89	
90	- **Give the clock two modes and pick deliberately.** A fixed instant is right for a resting
91	  state. A requirement about what the *passage* of time changes needs the clock installed and
92	  paused instead, so the page's timers exist and can be wound forward on purpose — a fixed clock
93	  has no timers to advance.
94	
95	## Fonts decide the layout, and the machine decides the fonts
96	
97	- **Vendoring the web fonts is half the job — every glyph they lack is drawn from the machine.**
98	  An emoji, an arrow, a currency sign, a non-Latin title: each falls back to whatever the host
99	  has installed, so the rendering quietly becomes a record of that machine's font set. The
100	  failure is brutal and unobvious — one string measures wider on a runner than on a workstation,
101	  wraps, and every card below it moves down a line. Launch the browser with its own
102	  font-configuration world whose only font directory is one you vendored, with the generic
103	  families aliased into it, so nothing installed on the host can reach the page.
104	
105	- **Ask the browser for reproducible rasterisation.** Disable hinting and subpixel text, force
106	  an sRGB colour profile, hide scrollbars, and disable GPU rasterisation. Shadows and blurs need
107	  two more: partial raster reuses tiles whose seams land inside a blur, and runtime-optimised
108	  drawing routines differ by CPU — both make the *same* page render differently run to run on
109	  one machine.
110	
111	## Capturing
112	
113	- **Wait on something the page itself produces, never on the network going quiet.** A selector
114	  that only exists once data rendered, or text that only appears once an async read returned, is
115	  a real signal; "no requests for a moment" is a guess that is wrong in both directions. Await
116	  font readiness too — text laid out before the fonts land is a different image.
117	
118	- **Clip at an element's box rather than screenshotting the element.** An element screenshot
119	  scrolls the element into view first, and a scroll dismisses whatever hover or focus opened the
120	  state you came to capture. A clip moves nothing. For the same reason, open hover-driven UI at
121	  capture time rather than in a preceding drive step, and settle the scroll position
122	  deliberately before measuring anything.
123	
124	- **A bounding box is viewport-space and goes stale.** Drivers scroll an element into view
125	  before clicking it, so a rectangle measured before a click means somewhere else after one.
126	  Convert to document coordinates at the moment of measurement, then take the clip from a
127	  full-page shot so a region below the fold is still inside the rendered image.
128	
129	- **Round a clip to whole pixels.** A layout rectangle is fractional; letting a fractional clip
130	  reach the screenshot leaves the rounding to the renderer, and half a pixel either way is a
131	  different image. Clamp it to the page's own bounds as well — a clip outside the rendered image
132	  is an error, not a crop.
133	
134	- **Rendering a shipped page outside its runtime means removing the scripts that need that
135	  runtime.** They throw on the first missing global and populate nothing, so the capture is of
136	  an empty surface that looks like a product bug. Strip them after load and set the state you
137	  meant to show yourself.
138	
139	- **Launch once and reuse the browser across captures.** Process startup dominates the cost of a
140	  capture, so a fresh browser per shot turns a fast run into a slow one for nothing; take a new
141	  context or page per capture instead, and close it, so no state leaks between them.
142

  has to be trusted.

- **Route a vendored third-party asset host-agnostically.** A stylesheet you serve in place of a
  CDN copy still resolves *its own* relative URLs against the host it was served from, so the
  font or image files it references arrive addressed to that CDN. Match those follow-up requests
  on the path alone, on any host, or the sheet loads and every asset it names 404s — which
  renders as a silent fallback rather than an error.

- **Know which knobs are fixed at context creation and which are per page.** Locale, timezone,
  viewport, device scale factor, geolocation and permissions belong to the browser *context* and
  cannot be changed once it exists — so proving that a product reads a fixed zone rather than
  the device's takes **two** contexts, not one page reconfigured twice. The clock, seeded
  randomness and injected scripts are per page.

- **A command-line window-size flag is not a viewport — a narrow one does not test the narrow
  layout.** Ask a browser's *CLI* for a phone-sized window and it renders the page at a clamped
  width and crops the overflow, without applying the media queries the width should have
  triggered. The output looks exactly like a horizontal-overflow bug in every section of a page
  that has none, and the instinct is to go hunting through the CSS for the offender. Only a
  context or page created with an explicit viewport puts the page in that layout. Reserve the
  CLI screenshot for the width the window happens to be, and give it a virtual-time budget that
  outlasts the page's entrance animations, or sections capture mid-transition and read as broken
  when they are fine.

- **Install every fake as an init script, so it runs before the page's first script.** A stub
  installed after load has already lost every call made during boot. Seeded randomness, storage
  seeds, and any API you are replacing all belong there.

- **Freezing CSS animation does not freeze the Web Animations API.** Zeroing
  `animation-duration` and `transition-duration` stops declarative animation and nothing else;
  anything driven through `element.animate` keeps running, and a capture races it. Stub the
  method so every such animation resolves on its end state immediately.

- **Give the clock two modes and pick deliberately.** A fixed instant is right for a resting
  state. A requirement about what the *passage* of time changes needs the clock installed and
  paused instead, so the page's timers exist and can be wound forward on purpose — a fixed clock
  has no timers to advance.

## Fonts decide the layout, and the machine decides the fonts

- **Vendoring the web fonts is half the job — every glyph they lack is drawn from the machine.**
  An emoji, an arrow, a currency sign, a non-Latin title: each falls back to whatever the host
  has installed, so the rendering quietly becomes a record of that machine's font set. The
  failure is brutal and unobvious — one string measures wider on a runner than on a workstation,
  wraps, and every card below it moves down a line. Launch the browser with its own
  font-configuration world whose only font directory is one you vendored, with the generic
  families aliased into it, so nothing installed on the host can reach the page.

- **Ask the browser for reproducible rasterisation.** Disable hinting and subpixel text, force
  an sRGB colour profile, hide scrollbars, and disable GPU rasterisation. Shadows and blurs need
  two more: partial raster reuses tiles whose seams land inside a blur, and runtime-optimised
  drawing routines differ by CPU — both make the *same* page render differently run to run on
  one machine.

## Capturing

- **Wait on something the page itself produces, never on the network going quiet.** A selector
  that only exists once data rendered, or text that only appears once an async read returned, is
  a real signal; "no requests for a moment" is a guess that is wrong in both directions. Await
  font readiness too — text laid out before the fonts land is a different image.

- **Clip at an element's box rather than screenshotting the element.** An element screenshot
  scrolls the element into view first, and a scroll dismisses whatever hover or focus opened the
  state you came to capture. A clip moves nothing. For the same reason, open hover-driven UI at
  capture time rather than in a preceding drive step, and settle the scroll position
  deliberately before measuring anything.

- **A bounding box is viewport-space and goes stale.** Drivers scroll an element into view
  before clicking it, so a rectangle measured before a click means somewhere else after one.
  Convert to document coordinates at the moment of measurement, then take the clip from a
  full-page shot so a region below the fold is still inside the rendered image.

- **Round a clip to whole pixels.** A layout rectangle is fractional; letting a fractional clip
  reach the screenshot leaves the rounding to the renderer, and half a pixel either way is a
  different image. Clamp it to the page's own bounds as well — a clip outside the rendered image
  is an error, not a crop.

- **Rendering a shipped page outside its runtime means removing the scripts that need that
  runtime.** They throw on the first missing global and populate nothing, so the capture is of
  an empty surface that looks like a product bug. Strip them after load and set the state you
  meant to show yourself.

- **Launch once and reuse the browser across captures.** Process startup dominates the cost of a
  capture, so a fresh browser per shot turns a fast run into a slow one for nothing; take a new
  context or page per capture instead, and close it, so no state leaks between them.

1	// The headless-browser pack: driving a real browser from your own process —
2	// resolving and pinning the build, replacing everything about the page's world
3	// that would otherwise vary, and the capture mechanics. Prose only, and
4	// deliberately so: every rule here is a RUNTIME browser behaviour (a secure
5	// origin gating geolocation, font fallback deciding layout, a scroll dismissing
6	// a hover state) or an authoring judgment about a harness's shape. Neither has a
7	// repo-state signature a check could read without asserting that some particular
8	// call still exists, which pins a point in time rather than a rule.
9	//
10	// Fingerprinted by an actual driver reference in JS/TS source — the module
11	// specifier of a browser-automation package, or a `.launch(` call site — so a
12	// repo that drives a browser from a globally-installed driver (no dependency
13	// entry anywhere) is still recognised. The marker only *suspects* the pack;
14	// declaring it is the project's call, like every pack.
15	
16	const DRIVER_MODULE = /['"](playwright(?:-core)?|puppeteer(?:-core)?)['"]/;
17	const LAUNCH_CALL = /\b(?:chromium|firefox|webkit|puppeteer)\.launch\s*\(/;
18	const SOURCE = /\.(mjs|cjs|js|jsx|ts|tsx)$/;
19	
20	export default {
21	  version: '60902.1',
22	  minEngineVersion: '60822.1',
23	  ruleRoutingGuidance: {
24	    belongs:
25	      'driving a real browser from code — resolving and pinning the build, faking the page world, capture mechanics',
26	    excludes:
27	      'which engine a UI golden needs and its review gate — basics writing-tests; workflow wiring — git-github',
28	  },
29	  marker: 'a browser-automation driver (playwright / puppeteer, or a .launch( call) referenced in JS/TS source',
30	  detect: (ctx) =>
31	    ctx.tracked.some((f) => {
32	      if (!SOURCE.test(f)) return false;
33	      const text = ctx.read(f);
34	      return text !== null && (DRIVER_MODULE.test(text) || LAUNCH_CALL.test(text));
35	    }),
36	};

236	  acknowledgements) and that you cross-checked against the full text — so a later

annotated overlay, a legend. Extract and describe it in the notes; a summary
  built from the prose alone silently omits it, and the omission is invisible
  until someone re-opens the source.
- **Write down what the source *fails* to say**, as an explicit gap list — the
  parameters, thresholds and units it never states. Recording an absence is what
  stops the next reader re-opening the source to hunt for something that was
  never in it. The intake is done when the notes make the original redundant, and
  a stated gap is part of that.
- **Explicitly record where your approach diverges from the reference and why.**
- **State what you deliberately omitted** (material not relevant to the
  algorithm — e.g. procedural/experimental setup detail, incidental statistics,
  acknowledgements) and that you cross-checked against the full text — so a later
  reader trusts the summary is complete for its purpose.
- Note that upload paths for source PDFs are **session-specific and won't
  persist**; the notes file is the durable artifact, not the upload.

## Keep signing and notarization an optional, secret-gated lane

- **The unsigned path must stay a working path.** Gate the Developer ID + notarization steps on the
  signing secrets being present, and ship an **ad-hoc-signed** artifact when they aren't. Make
  signing a required step and every fork, and every build in a repo whose secrets aren't set, goes
  red for a reason unrelated to the change.
- **An ad-hoc signature cannot be notarized.** They are separate lanes, not degrees of the same
  one: only an identity-signed bundle can be submitted to the notary service. Don't write a
  pipeline that "tries" to notarize whatever it just signed.
- **Notarize the distributed container, then staple it** (`notarytool submit --wait`, then `stapler
  staple` and `stapler validate`). Stapling is what makes the download open offline without a
  round-trip to Apple; skipping it works on your machine and fails on a user's.
- **In CI, an imported identity must be in the searchable keychain list.** Creating an ephemeral
  keychain, importing the `.p12` and setting the key partition list is not enough —
  `codesign` searches the *user's keychain list*, so the new keychain has to be added to it or the
  identity is simply not found.
- **Say out loud, in a build annotation, which lane ran.** "No signing secret — publishing an
  ad-hoc build" turns a silently-degraded artifact into a visible one.

## Distribution and the Gatekeeper story you owe the user

- **A drag-to-install DMG is a staged folder, not Finder scripting.** Stage the `.app` beside a
  symlink to `/Applications`, drop the icon in as `.VolumeIcon.icns`, flag the folder as having a
  custom icon, and let `hdiutil create` carry it through. Anything that automates Finder to lay out

1	import { existsSync, readFileSync } from 'node:fs';
2	import { join } from 'node:path';
3	import { finding } from './findings.mjs';
4	import { parseYaml } from './minimal-yaml.mjs';
5	import { stripComments } from './code-scanning.mjs';
6	import { normalizeEdges, barrierFindings, staleFindings } from './reference-scanning.mjs';
7	
8	// The declarative pattern-check engine: a rule whose whole logic is "these
9	// patterns over these files" is DECLARED as data — and data is JSON, not code.
10	// A pack's declarations live in `packs/<pack>/declared-checks.json` (a skill's
11	// in `<pack>/skills/<name>/declared-checks.json`), an array of specs the pack
12	// registry discovers structurally and compiles here into ordinary
13	// `{ id, severity, why, run(ctx) }` rule objects the runner treats like any
14	// other. Nothing wires them: dropping a declaration into the file adds it.
15	//
16	// The format admits no comments — the pattern plus its failureMessage/what/fix
17	// text IS the check — and no prose pointers: a declaration states its own case
18	// or it isn't finished. So a spec carries exactly:
19	//   id              the rule id settings and findings name it by
20	//   severity        'blocking' | 'advisory'
21	//   since           optional 'YYYY-MM-DD' — the date this check was added. A
22	//                   blocking check is enforced as advisory for its first
23	//                   GRACE_DAYS from it (helpers/findings.mjs), so a check can
24	//                   land against a tree that still violates it.
25	//   failureMessage  why this matters, printed on every finding the rule makes
26	//   …the assertions below, each with the `what` and `fix` it fails with
27	//
28	// REGEXES ARE STRINGS in `/body/flags` form — "/^\\s*schedule:/m" — compiled at
29	// load. Keys that accept a path instead (scanFiles, excludeFiles, pathExists)
30	// read any other string as an exact repo path; at every other pattern key a
31	// string that is not in `/…/` form is an authoring error, reported as one.
32	// The engine owns only the walking (the mechanism/policy line line-scanning.mjs
33	// draws): every pattern, file filter, and failure text stays in the declaration.
34	// Spec keys are deliberately wordy — a declaration must read as the whole check
35	// without this header.
36	//
37	// Built for MANY such rules at once: however many pattern rules a run holds,
38	// the engine makes ONE pass over the scanned tree — each file is read once and
39	// its lines split once, with every subscribing rule's assertions evaluated in
40	// that single visit — and the per-context results are cached, so the first
41	// pattern rule the runner reaches pays for the whole family and the rest are
42	// lookups. Regexes must be non-global (`.test` on a /g regex is stateful).
43	//
44	// A key the vocabulary cannot place is DROPPED at load, not thrown on: it is a
45	// typo (asserting nothing, silently) or a key a newer engine knows, and the load
46	// cannot tell them apart. Refusing it would wedge the second case — a member's
47	// pack lane and engine lane converge on separate cycles, so a declaration can
48	// legitimately reach an engine older than its vocabulary, and the converge that
49	// would deliver the newer engine is itself gated on the load (#1400). The typo is
50	// caught instead by the `declared-check-spec-keys` world rule, advisory where the
51	// skew is possible and blocking in the canon, where engine and declarations ship
52	// from one commit. A key the engine DOES place keeps its loud failure on a broken
53	// value (an uncompilable regex, a malformed date): that is not skew, it is broken.
54	//
55	// The spec vocabulary — everything beyond the rule metadata is optional:
56	//   fix                rule-level default: any assertion declaring `what` but
57	//                      no `fix` of its own inherits this one (for rules whose
58	//                      every assertion shares one remedy)
59	//   scope              "work" = this declaration judges the CHANGE rather than
60	//                      the repo, so it runs in check_the_work and may carry the
61	//                      work assertions below. Absent = world scope, the default
62	//                      (the pack manifest's own two rule lists say the same
63	//                      thing for a coded rule — a declaration has no list to
64	//                      sit in, so it states its scope here)
65	//   scanFiles          which files the content assertions read, in one of three
66	//                      forms: a RegExp over repo paths, one exact path (read
67	//                      directly), or an object naming the files ANOTHER parsed
68	//                      document points at —
69	//                        { inParsedFilesMatching, whereFileContains,
70	//                          namedByField, defaultingTo, withSuffix }
71	//                      every tracked document `inParsedFilesMatching` (refined
72	//                      by the `whereFileContains` probe) is parsed, the string
73	//                      at `namedByField` read from it — an array anywhere along
74	//                      that field path fans out over its entries, and
75	//                      `defaultingTo` supplies the name when the field's own
76	//                      parent is there without it — and each name, plus any
77	//                      `withSuffix`, resolved against the NAMING file's
78	//                      directory. A name pointing outside the scan set is
79	//                      dropped silently: a check has nothing to say about a
80	//                      file this checkout does not carry
81	//   scanFileClasses    named shared file sets widening the scan scope (unioned
82	//                      with a RegExp scanFiles): javascriptFiles, pythonFiles,
83	//                      markdownFiles, workflowFiles, testFiles
84	//   excludeFileClasses named shared file sets removed from scope (the same
85	//                      class names — testFiles is the usual one)
86	//   scanIgnoringComments  true = content assertions (matchLines, checkEachFile,
87	//                      repoWide, and requireIndexCoverage's whoseTextMatches)
88	//                      read each file with its JS/TS comments blanked
89	//                      (string-aware, line count preserved — code-scanning.mjs
90	//                      stripComments), so a comment merely naming a forbidden
91	//                      token never fires
92	//   scanIgnoringMarkdownFences  true = content assertions read each markdown
93	//                      file with its fenced code blocks blanked (line count
94	//                      preserved — the view checkSections always gets), so an
95	//                      example inside a fence never satisfies or trips a
96	//                      pattern; non-markdown files are untouched
97	//   scanTracked        true = scan every git-tracked file (mode-independent);
98	//                      default is ctx.files (the run's scanned set —
99	//                      tracked+untracked minus vendored, and only the changed
100	//                      files under --changed)
101	//   excludeFiles       RegExp (or exact path) removing files from scope
102	//   relevantWhen       repo-level relevance, all parts must hold:
103	//                        pathExists / pathAbsent          a path present/absent
104	//                        trackedFileMatches               some tracked path matches
105	//                        noTrackedFileMatches             no tracked path matches
106	//                        exactlyOneTrackedFileMatches     exactly one tracked path matches
107	//                        someTrackedFileContains          { pathMatching, text,
108	//                                                           ignoringComments } — some
109	//                                                         tracked path matching the first
110	//                                                         has text matching the second
111	//                                                         (ignoringComments: true reads it
112	//                                                         with JS/TS comments blanked)
113	//                        scanningWholeRepo                true = only under a whole-repo
114	//                                                         sweep (mode 'all'), never a
115	//                                                         --changed run
116	//                        repoContains                     some in-scope file's text
117	//                                                         matches — evaluated only
118	//                                                         if findings exist
119	//   whenMissing        { what, fix } — fires when an exact-path scanFiles is absent
120	//   maxLines           { limit, what, fix } — fires past `limit` lines, anchored there
121	//   maxLineLength      { bytes, what, fix } — one finding per file whose lines
122	//                      run past `bytes` (UTF-8 bytes, so wide characters count
123	//                      what they cost), anchored at the first over-long line;
124	//                      {count}/{longest}/{bytes} interpolate
125	//   skipLinesMatching  RegExp — lines it matches are invisible to matchLines
126	//   matchLines         [{ match, andLineMatches, unlessLineMatches,
127	//                         unlessPreviousLineMatches,
128	//                         andIndentedBlockBelowMatches,
129	//                         unlessIndentedBlockBelowMatches,
130	//                         andWithinBlockOpenedBy, unlessWithinBlockOpenedBy,
131	//                         whenPathMatches,
132	//                         whenFileMatches, unlessFileMatches, what, fix }]
133	//                      flag each line `match` hits — provided `andLineMatches`
134	//                      (if declared) also hits it, `unlessLineMatches` does
135	//                      not, and `unlessPreviousLineMatches` does not hit the
136	//                      line above (the first line has none) — in files whose
137	//                      path matches `whenPathMatches` (absent = every scanned
138	//                      file), where every `whenFileMatches` matches the text
139	//                      and `unlessFileMatches` does not; per line, the first
140	//                      matching assertion wins.
141	//                      The four BLOCK relations read the indentation structure

# headless-browser pack

Active when the repo references a browser-automation driver in JS/TS source — a `playwright` /
`playwright-core` / `puppeteer` / `puppeteer-core` module specifier, or a `.launch(` call site.
Scanning source rather than a dependency manifest is deliberate: a repo can drive a browser its
environment image already installs, with no dependency entry anywhere to find.

Prose only. Every rule is a runtime browser behaviour or a judgment about a harness's shape,
neither of which has a repo-state signature a check could read without asserting that a
particular call still exists — the shape the corpus rejects outright.

## Rules (`RULES.md`)

| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Resolve binary, never download | high | correctness | prose: 123 words |
| Reinstalling the driver repeats the download danger | high | correctness | prose: 130 words |
| Stub an unvendored CDN library's API | medium | correctness | prose: 114 words |
| Pin the build for pixels | high | correctness | prose: 87 words |
| Zero-diff costs whole recipe | medium | correctness | prose: 95 words |
| Fake origin, abort by default | high | correctness | prose: 80 words |
| `https` origin for geolocation | medium | correctness | prose: 48 words |
| Route vendored assets host-agnostically | medium | correctness | prose: 75 words |
| Context knobs vs page knobs | medium | correctness | prose: 67 words |
| Window-size flag isn't a viewport | high | correctness | prose: 132 words |
| Fakes as init scripts | high | correctness | prose: 42 words |
| CSS freeze misses `element.animate` | high | correctness | prose: 45 words |
| Two clock modes | medium | correctness | prose: 55 words |
| Font jail, not just webfonts | high | correctness | prose: 111 words |
| Reproducible rasterisation flags | high | correctness | prose: 60 words |
| Wait on the page's signal | high | correctness | prose: 66 words |
| Clip, don't screenshot the element | medium | correctness | prose: 65 words |
| Bounding boxes go stale | medium | correctness | prose: 59 words |
| Whole-pixel clips | medium | correctness | prose: 57 words |
| Strip scripts needing the runtime | medium | correctness | prose: 53 words |
| One browser, many contexts | medium | performance | prose: 51 words |

## Boundary

This pack is the browser itself. Which engine a UI golden should use, the tolerance it may carry,
self-skipping where no browser is present, the re-baselining approval gate, and wiring the run into
a workflow are all deliberately not here — the "zero-diff costs the whole recipe" rule is written to
complement that testing guidance rather than restate or contradict it.

Provenance: distilled from three fleet members that drive a browser from code, independently and
for different reasons. `missingbulb/EdFringeNow` — a pinned-Chromium visual-requirements harness:
fake-origin routing, the font jail, rasterisation flags, clip and bounding-box mechanics.
`missingbulb/CrosswordChat` — browser rasterisation for both goldens and generated build
artifacts: environment binary resolution, stripping runtime-dependent scripts.
`missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite` — an interactive responsive check: the window-size-is-not-a-
viewport footgun and the virtual-time budget. The first two solved the cross-machine rendering
problem two different ways, which is what the pinning rules carry.
`missingbulb/EdFringeAllocator` holds a vestigial fourth instance in a retired prototype.

content.content: 3:Each `packs//` bundles a pack's **prose** (`RULES.md`, injected at session start when the pack is active), its **checks** (run at every Stop), and its **bundled skills** (`/skills/`, mounted at session start). **No pack is active by default** — every pack, the `basics` baseline included, activates only when declared in `.claudinite-settings.json` (bootstrap's `--init` seeds `basics` plus the fingerprinted technology packs; the nightly update backfills the explicit `basics` declaration into existing consumers). Discovery is structural — any `packs//pack.mjs` is a pack, and that manifest is the pack's index: what it owns, the checks it runs in each scope, the skills it bundles. A pack's `README.md` is **optional** and carries only what the manifest cannot — provenance, design rationale, an index of its prose. A README that restates the manifest is duplication with a drift risk, and several had already drifted. 18:| [basics](basics/README.md) | declared (seeded by `--init`) | 15 | 58 (working-discipline + task-lifecycle, plus the [folder-access graph](basics/barriers.md) and the weekly comment pass; 2 path-forced skills: writing-repo-scanning-checks, working-with-generated-files) | 20:| [claudinite-growth](claudinite-growth/README.md) | declared (seeded by `--init`, opt-out by removal) | 1 | 0 — growth member-side tasks (extract over activity + conversations / dedup / pack discovery / prose-to-checks) + in-session merge capture | 24:| [claudinite-canon-curation](claudinite-canon-curation/README.md) | declared (opt-in; a canon home repo only, and `hidden` from the consumer catalog) | 2 | 26 (curating a canon — the central promote stage, the weekly fleet pack-discovery sweep, the monthly upstream reconciliation, the pack version cut on the base branch with its derived history, and the shelf's own policing: naming, config, modules, checks and prose; 2 skills: generate-project-instructions, writing-claudinite-skills) | 31:| [headless-browser](headless-browser/README.md) | driver reference in JS/TS source | 0 | 18 | 55:`.claudinite/local/packs//` — the same slots (prose `RULES.md`, `rules` checks, `skills`, 67: same one shape canon packs use); a bundled skill may carry `checks.mjs`, run when the pack is 72:A local pack contributes **every** slot first-class: prose, checks, skills, **and scheduled 84:The `"packs"` list and the rest of `.claudinite-settings.json` are validated **when the file loads**, not by a conformance check: [`loadConfig`](../engine/checks/helpers/repo-context.mjs) reports malformed JSON and an unknown top-level property, and the runner adds an unknown *pack name* (it holds the registry). Each becomes a blocking `config` error — a wrong pack name is as much a settings error as invalid JSON. A pack's `detect`/`marker` only **suspects** a pack is wanted; declaring it is the project's call, so a declared pack without its marker (or a marker without its declaration) is **not** flagged. 96:Reporting is not fatal: a pack whose declaration is incomplete still loads and still runs its checks. Silently disabling a repo's own rules is a worse failure than the one being reported. The field vocabulary is **closed** — an undeclared key is an error, so a typo (`rule:`, `skill:`) fails loudly instead of being ignored forever. 148:A pack's coded checks live in two directories, and **which directory a rule sits in is what makes it world- or work-scoped**: `/worldRules/*.mjs` audit repo state ([`check_the_world`](../engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs)), `/workRules/*.mjs` judge the change and session in front of you ([`check_the_work`](../engine/checks/check_the_work.mjs)). Each module default-exports one rule, and the loader imports them in filename order — discovered structurally, exactly like the `declared-checks.json` beside them, so adding a check is writing its file and nothing else. The loader flattens both scopes into the single `rules` array the runners walk, stamping each rule's scope from the directory it came from — one derivation, nothing downstream re-decides it. A rule module that carries its own `scope` field is a second source for the same fact, free to contradict its own placement, so the spec rejects it. 152:A skill's own `checks.mjs` sits outside this partition (it is a skill's content, not a manifest list) and still declares `scope` on the rule itself. 158:The SessionStart hook [`../engine/pack_loader/mount-skills.mjs`](../engine/pack_loader/mount-skills.mjs) mounts the **union over the active packs' bundles** (same activation as prose/checks/env) as session-generated `.claude/skills/` symlinks — nothing committed, and a self-ignoring `.claude/skills/.gitignore` keeps them out of git status. A skill rides its pack everywhere the pack goes: the vendor set, the mounts, the sweep (its `checks.mjs` runs when the pack is active). Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/writing-tests

# Testing practices

A consuming repo's own test *mechanics* — runner, layout, which suites exist — are its own docs'; CI-trigger rules and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` workflow-recursion gotcha are [git-github-advanced](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md)'s.

- See a test fail before you trust it: write it red before the fix (green after), or break what it guards and watch it go red. A test that has never failed proves nothing. For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. See-it-fail there **must** be the second method — mutate the new guard (weaken it), watch the test bite, then restore it. Restore with `git checkout -- <file>` (or `git stash`) taken at the moment of mutating — never a `.bak` copy saved earlier, which predates whatever else you edited in between and silently discards that intervening work. If the mutation was **staged** (to make a check that scans `git diff --cached` fire), a bare `git checkout -- <file>` restores from the index — which now holds the mutation — so the "restore" is a no-op; use `git checkout HEAD -- <file>` (or `git reset` first).
- A mechanism meant to survive a retry, re-queue, or hand-off needs a test that calls it twice, not once. A suite of single-call tests stays green while the multi-call case corrupts state — the double-call is what a real retry, requeue, or hand-off actually does. When the mechanism arbitrates by identity (a claim, a lock), the second call must come from a **different actor**: a single actor retrying its own stale claim can't expose an identity-masked race, since it still recognizes its own claim as valid.
- A simulator of a stateful mechanism must advance state only where the real engine's code actually leaves a mark — never wherever the rule's stated description says a transition happens. A sim that fires on every event matching the rule's *intent* is correct by construction against that rule and blind to exactly the silent paths where the real implementation and the rule have quietly diverged — which is where a genuine bug usually lives. Read the real engine's code for what it *writes*, and model that.
- Before trusting a new transform/normalizer, run it over the *real existing corpus* it will process, not just hand-picked test inputs — the live data exposes edge cases your examples won't. Relatedly, prefer a generic structural rule over a hand-maintained list of special cases: the enumerated list needs per-instance upkeep and silently has gaps, while a rule keyed on structure (e.g. "a known registry label under any 2-letter ccTLD") covers the whole class at once. (3)
- A test that stubs the exact boundary where the bug lives can't catch that bug — it guards only the shape it asserts, not the runtime effect. Say what it can't catch.
- A test that dereferences a path inside a **read-only dependency tree someone else refreshes** — a vendored mount, a synced submodule, generated output from an upstream build — is a test whose fixture a stranger can delete: the day upstream retires that file the case fails `ENOENT` with nothing in your repo having changed. Assert against a path only when the test itself creates it; when a case genuinely needs an upstream file, read it **defensively** and skip with a stated reason if it is gone, so a retirement upstream reports as "no longer applicable" rather than as your repo being broken. Check what actually runs these cases too — a suite that the repo's own gate never invokes reports its breakage to whoever happens to look.
- **Never test that a value is set.** A test that reads a value someone declared — a config or manifest field (`assert.equal(task.expected_outcome, 'fresh_pr')`), an exported constant or default object (`assert.deepEqual(DEFAULTS, {…})`), a settings file naming a pack, a workflow's `run:` line, a frontmatter key — and asserts it is the literal it was set to restates the file under test in a second file. It can only fail when someone changes the value **on purpose**, so it catches no defect and instead taxes every deliberate change with a mirrored edit — and teaches that the value is load-bearing prose to be restated, which is how one setting ends up copied into a comment, a worker doc, a README table and a test, so flipping it becomes a five-file diff. The see-it-fail test exposes it: to make the assertion go red you must break the thing it asserts, which is not a bug. "It exists", "it has the right shape" and "it is one of these" are the same test in a looser coat. Test the **behaviour the value drives** instead: feed the real code the declared value and assert what the code does with it — a task declared `weekly` is planned once across a fourteen-day clock, a check declared over `**/*.mjs` fires on a fixture `.mjs` and stays silent on a `.md`, a default object yields the documented output when nothing overrides it. Where no code reads the value there is nothing to test; if a declaration genuinely must not change without deliberation, that is a review concern, not a test. What *does* earn an assertion on declared data is a claim spanning two artifacts that could drift independently: the doc a field *names* exists; every signal the code reads is declared; two implementations of the same list agree; a value the runtime constrains is inside its legal set — proven by running the constraint, not by re-listing the set.
- **Testing a task's precondition or declaration** — assert only the pack's own code: a
  task-local term's decisions, a worker's behaviour, or a composition it designed; a plain
  built-in term or a validated declaration is the scheduler's own mechanism, proved once by its
  own suite.
- Prefer a single shared double; but when a subsystem is faked by more than one (a minimal unit stub vs. a faithful harness that boots the real module), a new call into the faked surface must be taught to **every** double, or the untaught one breaks — and the faithful harness turns an unmodeled API into a confusing **far-away** failure (a DOM-snapshot pixel-diff, not a local error at the call site). After adding a call into a faked boundary, find every double of it and extend each.
- When one wire format, encoding, or algorithm is **implemented twice** — two languages, two tiers, a hand-rolled client encoder against the server's library — no compiler, type system, or single test run spans the two, so the only thing holding them together is a **shared vector set carried deliberately by both suites**: the same inputs and the same expected outputs, asserted independently on each side, including the boundary cases the two could plausibly round differently (a value exactly on a bisection midpoint, a tie, a truncation edge). A vector asserted on only one side is an input nobody ever compared — both suites stay green, in different languages under different runners, while the claim quietly stops covering it. So: touching *either* implementation re-runs *both* suites, and adding a vector adds it to both. Where the pairing is mechanical (the two vector lists must contain the same inputs), pin it with a check rather than a convention.
- A traceability/coverage gate that requires every spec item be *claimed* by some test of one fixed kind proves only that it's claimed, not that it's verified. When items differ in kind, the gate green-lights claims that kind can't check — a pixel snapshot "covers" a click's tab-opening it can never observe, or a state the case never renders (and can't, when the data can't reach it). Segment the gate by the verification each item needs (route behavior to a behavior test, rendering to a snapshot) rather than forcing every item onto one mechanism. (1)
- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). Thread the reference time through the code under test, defaulting to the real clock in production. When retrofitting such a rule into an existing fixture suite, pin the reference instant so existing fixtures land on the same side they were authored for — so only the cases that deliberately exercise the new rule change and the diff stays small and reviewable, rather than a sprawling baseline churn that buries the intended change.
- A round-trip test that asserts by comparing **serialized** forms (`JSON.stringify(decoded) === JSON.stringify(original)`) silently makes key *order* part of the contract: add a field at the top of the encoder's record and append it in the decoder's, and the round-trip fails on ordering alone — with a diff that reads like a data bug and sends you after a value that was correct all along. Deep-equal the parsed structures instead, so the test states what it means; keep serialized comparison only where byte-identity is genuinely the property under test, and say so in the test.
- A new **e2e / heavy-browser** test must go green at least twice in CI before merging — one green run doesn't rule out a flake. This applies only to that class (the real-Chrome `test/fullBrowserHeavyTests/` suites); the deterministic offline/unit/integration tests don't touch a live browser or network, so one green run is enough for them.
- A test that can only run remotely (e.g. CI-only) must diagnose itself: on failure, dump the observed state, not just an assertion. It must also be *hang-proof* — bound every `await` (a timeout race) and set a test-level timeout — so a failure fails fast with that diagnostic instead of burning the whole job's timeout. An unbounded await on something that never settles (e.g. a callback that silently never fires) turns a 5-second failure into a 20-minute hang, and each CI-only iteration already costs a full round-trip.
- Run a suite you know is slow as **its own command with an explicit timeout well above its measured runtime**, and do the dependency install as a *separate, earlier* call. An agent shell caps a command at a default (order of a couple of minutes) and pushes it to the background when it expires; the reflex is then to start the suite over, so one green result costs double the wall clock with two suites racing each other. Chaining setup in front of the suite is what usually pushes the pair past the cap. If a run does get backgrounded, wait on the one already running rather than launching a second.
- To test code that drives a real browser or other external runtime in CI, prefer a *self-authored hermetic input* (e.g. a `data:` URL whose own script reproduces the behavior) over hitting a live third-party target — the live target is non-deterministic and often bot-blocked from a CI/datacenter IP, so it flakes or can't run, while a self-authored input exercises the same engine deterministically. (2)
- Gate a fuzzy quality metric (a coverage %, not a binary pass) behind a high-watermark: refresh the artifact and ratchet the watermark up locally, keep CI read-only (assert against the committed baseline, never rewrite it), and re-baseline by hand only when a deliberate change legitimately moves it — a number that can only climb catches a silent regression without flapping on noise. When the population it covers can *grow* (e.g. new test cases), store the set the watermark was computed over and gate only over the cases shared with it, so a newly added item is excluded rather than dragging the aggregate below the bar; re-anchor the watermark when the set changes. (A single aggregate watermark can then be re-anchored over a regression bundled into the *same* change as a set change — store per-item bars if that must be caught.)
- For behavior a person must sign off on (a third-party integration, an extraction result), keep a layer of declarative, human-reviewed expectation files — distinct from the unit tests, which nobody reads for *intent* — and cover every behavior change with a minimal, representative case there (one behavior per case, no incidental complexity), since that case is what gets reviewed.
- When a snapshot/golden test fails because the output *legitimately* moved (the pixels or bytes changed for a real reason), don't quietly regenerate the baseline to go green — an unreviewed baseline change is an unreviewed behavior change. Surface the diff (committed **expected**, newly-rendered **actual**, highlighted **diff**) and get owner approval before re-baselining; until then keep the *reverted* baseline committed so the branch honestly shows the test red-pending — never commit the new baseline first.
- When a test asserts exact values extracted from a captured artifact (a cached page, a recorded response), record and commit the artifact *first*, then read the expected values off the committed file — don't hand-write the expectations from memory or a live view and hope they match. Guessing the value desyncs the test from the real fixture; reading it off the committed bytes can't.
- A test that maintains a committed artifact should regenerate it into the working tree deterministically (no timestamps, so an unchanged run yields no diff) and skip the write under CI — never shell out to git from a test. Commit the artifact through the normal review flow, like a snapshot.
- Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. A surface that is inline-styled SVG, or flexbox-only markup authored for it, renders **bit-exact** through a headless rasterizer (e.g. satori → SVG, resvg → PNG) driven by the shipped code, using **bundled** fonts, never system fonts, and a pinned locale — demand a **zero-pixel** diff there. But that rasterizer has no CSS engine and draws no native widgets: a full shipped page using CSS **grid**, custom properties (`var()`), `@media`, **emoji**, or **form controls** (a range slider, radio, `<select>`) is beyond it — screenshot that with a **headless browser** instead, and allow a *small* diff tolerance (browser antialiasing varies across machines, so it isn't bit-exact). Match the engine to the surface; never reshape the product to fit the rasterizer. (A rasterized popup golden works only because the popup was authored flexbox-only — the moment a surface needs grid/vars/widgets, it needs a browser.) Since the browser goldens aren't gate-able bit-exact and a runner may lack the browser, let those cases **self-skip** where it's absent so the deterministic cases still gate.
- Reproduce a reported golden-image flake with the harness's own pixel comparator, never a raw byte or file-hash compare: a byte-hash is strictly tighter than a zero-pixel-diff comparator (it also fails on identical pixels re-encoded differently), so it manufactures "reproductions" of a flake that never fails the real gate.
- To image-golden a surface your code **injects into a host page** (a control mounted into a third-party toolbar), render it against a **committed capture of the real host DOM with its computed styles flattened inline** — the deterministic rasterizer reads only inline styles, and the host's own stylesheet is not yours to ship. Mount it with the **shipped injector** (so the golden proves the placement, not a hand-placed copy), and name the model's boundary honestly: substituted icon-font glyphs, an approximated host chrome (a captured sample is spec, not folklore — the origin lesson of a supported-targets matrix).

# Running the suite

- **The whole suite is one command** — `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`. There is no test
  script; `ci.yml`'s array is not authoritative. A bash glob without `globstar` is the dangerous
  substitute — it reached 37 of 65 files and reported nothing wrong — while `node --test <dir>`
  fails outright, so only the glob leaves you believing a green run. (4)
- **Read a run's output from a file** — redirect one run and grep that file for the slice you need;
  never re-run the ~55s suite to re-slice unchanged output. (1)
- **`git add` a new test file before certifying a run green** — `git ls-files` excludes an unstaged
  file, so the run never executed it; the `untracked-test-file` finding at Stop says which. (2)
- **Iterating on a sweep across many files** — run only the test files the edit touches, plus
  `check_the_work`; spend the whole suite and `check_the_world` once, at the end. Both are
  whole-tree aggregates whose verdict cannot turn on one file. (3)

# Writing a check that scans the repo

- **Choosing the file set** — take it from `git ls-files` rather than a filesystem walk with
  paths to skip, and remember a brand-new file is untracked until you add it, so a green run
  isn't coverage of it.

- **Scanning for a forbidden token** — strip comments first so it matches code, not prose —
  string-aware, since a `//` inside a URL is not a comment. Reuse `stripComments` from
  [`engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs`](../../../../engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs);
  if the scan can't import it, inline the same pass and point a comment back at that source.
  Strip in **both** directions — a comment that documents or warns about the banned pattern is
  exactly where a naive check trips over its own reasoning, so a commented-out instance must not
  count as present either.

- **Proving the check silent** — run it against the repo's own **real** sources, not only a
  synthetic clean fixture — a fixture spelling the same gap the check has just keeps proving the
  matching, and only a real-tree run can disagree with you.

# headless-browser pack

Active when the repo references a browser-automation driver in JS/TS source — a `playwright` /
`playwright-core` / `puppeteer` / `puppeteer-core` module specifier, or a `.launch(` call site.
Scanning source rather than a dependency manifest is deliberate: a repo can drive a browser its
environment image already installs, with no dependency entry anywhere to find.

Prose only. Every rule is a runtime browser behaviour or a judgment about a harness's shape,
neither of which has a repo-state signature a check could read without asserting that a
particular call still exists — the shape the corpus rejects outright.

## Rules (`RULES.md`)

| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Resolve binary, never download | high | correctness | prose: 123 words |
| Reinstalling the driver repeats the download danger | high | correctness | prose: 130 words |
| Stub an unvendored CDN library's API | medium | correctness | prose: 114 words |
| Pin the build for pixels | high | correctness | prose: 87 words |
| Zero-diff costs whole recipe | medium | correctness | prose: 95 words |
| Fake origin, abort by default | high | correctness | prose: 80 words |
| `https` origin for geolocation | medium | correctness | prose: 48 words |
| Route vendored assets host-agnostically | medium | correctness | prose: 75 words |
| Context knobs vs page knobs | medium | correctness | prose: 67 words |
| Window-size flag isn't a viewport | high | correctness | prose: 132 words |
| Fakes as init scripts | high | correctness | prose: 42 words |
| CSS freeze misses `element.animate` | high | correctness | prose: 45 words |
| Two clock modes | medium | correctness | prose: 55 words |
| Font jail, not just webfonts | high | correctness | prose: 111 words |
| Reproducible rasterisation flags | high | correctness | prose: 60 words |
| Wait on the page's signal | high | correctness | prose: 66 words |
| Clip, don't screenshot the element | medium | correctness | prose: 65 words |
| Bounding boxes go stale | medium | correctness | prose: 59 words |
| Whole-pixel clips | medium | correctness | prose: 57 words |
| Strip scripts needing the runtime | medium | correctness | prose: 53 words |
| One browser, many contexts | medium | performance | prose: 51 words |

## Boundary

This pack is the browser itself. Which engine a UI golden should use, the tolerance it may carry,
self-skipping where no browser is present, the re-baselining approval gate, and wiring the run into
a workflow are all deliberately not here — the "zero-diff costs the whole recipe" rule is written to
complement that testing guidance rather than restate or contradict it.

Provenance: distilled from three fleet members that drive a browser from code, independently and
for different reasons. `missingbulb/EdFringeNow` — a pinned-Chromium visual-requirements harness:
fake-origin routing, the font jail, rasterisation flags, clip and bounding-box mechanics.
`missingbulb/CrosswordChat` — browser rasterisation for both goldens and generated build
artifacts: environment binary resolution, stripping runtime-dependent scripts.
`missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite` — an interactive responsive check: the window-size-is-not-a-
viewport footgun and the virtual-time budget. The first two solved the cross-machine rendering
problem two different ways, which is what the pinning rules carry.
`missingbulb/EdFringeAllocator` holds a vestigial fourth instance in a retired prototype.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
# headless-browser pack

Active when the repo references a browser-automation driver in JS/TS source — a `playwright` /
`playwright-core` / `puppeteer` / `puppeteer-core` module specifier, or a `.launch(` call site.
Scanning source rather than a dependency manifest is deliberate: a repo can drive a browser its
environment image already installs, with no dependency entry anywhere to find.

Almost all prose. Nearly every rule is a runtime browser behaviour or a judgment about a harness's
shape, neither of which has a repo-state signature a check could read without asserting that a
particular call still exists — the shape the corpus rejects outright. The exception is the one
forbidden pattern: a browser path hardcoded to a build number, which pins nothing and names a
directory the next image rebuild replaces.

## Rules (`RULES.md`)

| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Resolve binary, never download | high | correctness | prose: 123 words + check (`headless-browser/version-stamped-browser-path`) |
| Reinstalling the driver repeats the download danger | high | correctness | prose: 130 words |
| Stub an unvendored CDN library's API | medium | correctness | prose: 114 words |
| Pin the build for pixels | high | correctness | prose: 87 words |
| Zero-diff costs whole recipe | medium | correctness | prose: 95 words |
| Fake origin, abort by default | high | correctness | prose: 80 words |
| `https` origin for geolocation | medium | correctness | prose: 48 words |
| Route vendored assets host-agnostically | medium | correctness | prose: 75 words |
| Context knobs vs page knobs | medium | correctness | prose: 67 words |
| Window-size flag isn't a viewport | high | correctness | prose: 132 words |
| Fakes as init scripts | high | correctness | prose: 42 words |
| CSS freeze misses `element.animate` | high | correctness | prose: 45 words |
| Two clock modes | medium | correctness | prose: 55 words |
| Font jail, not just webfonts | high | correctness | prose: 111 words |
| Reproducible rasterisation flags | high | correctness | prose: 60 words |
| Wait on the page's signal | high | correctness | prose: 66 words |
| Clip, don't screenshot the element | medium | correctness | prose: 65 words |
| Bounding boxes go stale | medium | correctness | prose: 59 words |
| Whole-pixel clips | medium | correctness | prose: 57 words |
| Strip scripts needing the runtime | medium | correctness | prose: 53 words |
| One browser, many contexts | medium | performance | prose: 51 words |

## Boundary

This pack is the browser itself. Which engine a UI golden should use, the tolerance it may carry,
self-skipping where no browser is present, the re-baselining approval gate, and wiring the run into
a workflow are all deliberately not here — the "zero-diff costs the whole recipe" rule is written to
complement that testing guidance rather than restate or contradict it.

Provenance: distilled from three fleet members that drive a browser from code, independently and
for different reasons. `missingbulb/EdFringeNow` — a pinned-Chromium visual-requirements harness:
fake-origin routing, the font jail, rasterisation flags, clip and bounding-box mechanics.
`missingbulb/CrosswordChat` — browser rasterisation for both goldens and generated build
artifacts: environment binary resolution, stripping runtime-dependent scripts.
`missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite` — an interactive responsive check: the window-size-is-not-a-
viewport footgun and the virtual-time budget. The first two solved the cross-machine rendering
problem two different ways, which is what the pinning rules carry.
`missingbulb/EdFringeAllocator` holds a vestigial fourth instance in a retired prototype.

input.body:
Two conversions from the worklist in [`docs/declarative-checks/rule-inventory.md`](../blob/main/docs/declarative-checks/rule-inventory.md), both **A** rows in packs that had never been swept against it.

## What converted

| Prose | Became | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| `packs/headless-browser/RULES.md` — *"Never hardcode the version-stamped path you found by looking: it moves with the next image, and the failure lands on whoever rebuilds rather than on whoever wrote it."* | **`headless-browser/version-stamped-browser-path`** | blocking (`since: 2026-09-13`) |
| `packs/macos/RULES.md` — *"Notarize the distributed container, then staple it (`notarytool submit --wait`, then `stapler staple`…)"* | **`notarytool-submit-waits`** | blocking (`since: 2026-09-13`) |

Both are declared checks — patterns over files, so neither earned a rule module.

**`headless-browser/version-stamped-browser-path`** is a forbidden pattern rather than an assertion that some call still exists, which is why it clears the bar the pack's own manifest set when it declared itself prose-only. It flags a path segment naming a browser directory stamped with a build number (`/ms-playwright/chromium-1148/…`, `/firefox-1482/…`) and the Chrome-for-Testing form whose stamp is the platform's (`/chrome/linux-131.0.6778.85/…`). The unstamped directories a real install carries — `chrome-linux64`, `chrome-headless-shell` — are quiet by construction, as is a pinned download URL, which names a release rather than an install root.

**`notarytool-submit-waits`** is file-scoped, not line-scoped, and deliberately: a real notarize command carries its flags on backslash continuations, so judging the `submit` line alone would flag the correct spelling. It fires where a script or workflow submits to the notary service and nothing anywhere in that file waits for the verdict — neither `--wait` nor an explicit `xcrun notarytool wait <id>`.

## See-it-fail

Every fixture proved red-first, then each false-positive guard mutated in turn and watched to bite, then restored.

- `packs/headless-browser/test/pack.test.mjs` — 9 cases (3 flagged, 6 quiet). Guards that bit: the two match patterns, the comment-blind view, the `#`-comment skip, the markdown exclusion, the unstamped-name structure, and the hyphen that separates a platform from its version.
- `packs/macos/test/notarytool-submit-waits.test.mjs` — 7 cases (2 flagged, 5 quiet). Guards that bit: the match, the file-scoped wait exemption and each of its two arms, the `#`-comment skip, and the scan scope.

One narrowing is worth naming: the comment-blind view is JS-aware, so an unquoted `//` in a shell or YAML line takes the rest of that line with it. That only ever produces silence, and the test file says so rather than spelling a fixture that would pass on the stripper instead of the pattern.

## Deletion test

**Nothing deleted — both paragraphs stay whole.** The headless-browser bullet also carries the resolution order and the `-core` preference; the macOS bullet also carries the staple itself, `stapler validate`, and why stapling is what makes the download open offline. Neither is covered by the check standing beside it.

## Green before the PR

3451 tests / 0 fail (3435 before, +16). `check_the_world` exit 0 — 0 blocking, 104 advisory, all pre-existing (`file-placement` ×89, `rules-line-length` ×12, `design-doc-status-banner` ×3); `check_the_work` silent. Neither new rule fires on this tree — this repo declares neither pack, and the only match either finds anywhere is inside its own fixture file.

## Also examined, left as prose

- **`playwright install` committed in a script or workflow** (the inventory's other half of the same row) — a repo whose CI runner ships no browser installs one there, and that is the documented step; flagging it would red correct work. **`@playwright/test` has no `-core` variant**, so the "prefer the `-core` package" half cannot be a check either. Both logged in the inventory row.
- **macOS "notarize then staple" as a pairing** — re-derived against today's tree and the 2026-08-16 rejection still holds: a scan sees both commands in one file, never that they name the same distributed container.
- Everything the 2026-07-26 → 2026-08-30 tracker entries already rejected was re-read and nothing material moved.

Logged on [#450](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/450). Refs #1962.
